# Incident Report: 2024-08-15 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim host
- **IPv4:** 10.8.15.133
- **MAC:** 00:1c:bf:03:54:82 (confirmed via ARP and as the Ethernet source on all traffic from that IP)
- **Windows hostname:** DESKTOP-H8ALZBV (DHCP option 12, NBNS, and Kerberos client principal `DESKTOP-H8ALZBV$` all agree)
- **Domain:** lafontainebleu.org (AD domain; DC is WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS at 10.8.15.4)
- **Logged-in user:** plucero (Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString `plucero` from 10.8.15.133)

## Malware family
Attribution confidence: **behavioral** (no AV/YARA signature check was run; no internet lookups were performed). The strongest identifying artifact is the PE debug path embedded in the second-stage payload:

```
E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb
```

This self-identifies the payload's internal build/project name as **"knock" v1.1.8**, a 64-bit DLL loader/backdoor. It is not a mainstream commodity-malware family name I could independently confirm without external threat-intel lookup, but the PDB string is direct evidence recovered from the binary itself. The delivery chain and C2 mechanics (fake-invoice phishing site → padded JScript downloader → BITS-fetched DLL → custom encrypted HTTP beacon) are consistent with a loader/backdoor used for follow-on payload delivery.

## Infection chain (all times relative to capture start, 2024-08-15 04:09:43 UTC)

| t (s) | Event |
|---|---|
| 74.7 | `GET http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=...&Ld=...` (Chrome/Edg 127 UA) → HTTP 200, `application/octet-stream`. Response is a ZIP archive containing `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js`, a 6.99 MB JScript file padded almost entirely with junk paragraph text (book/report excerpts) to inflate size and evade AV — a fake-FedEx-tracking phishing/malvertising lure. |
| 135.9–136.2 | `HEAD` then `GET http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4`, User-Agent `Microsoft BITS/7.8` (i.e., fetched via the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service, invoked by the JS downloader) → HTTP 200, 159,232-byte PE32+ (x86-64) DLL, mislabeled `text/html`. |
| 196.9 → 1962.0 (end of capture) | Persistent HTTP beaconing from 10.8.15.133 to 72.5.43.29:80 begins and continues for the rest of the capture: 308 requests over ~30 minutes, roughly every 6 seconds. Requests go to a bare IP address (no corresponding DNS query for 72.5.43.29 anywhere in the capture) with a spoofed User-Agent `Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)` (note the anomalous space before "5.0" — a distinguishing artifact of this loader). Each request carries a large base64 blob in a `Cookie:` header (host-identification/session token). Server responses use a custom named-field protocol: `CMD=POLL\nINFO=1\nACK=1` (keepalive) or `CMD=ENCD\nES=1\nDATA=<binary blob>` (encrypted command/data exchange); malformed exchanges get a plain `400 Bad Request`. |

## Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `72.5.43.29:80` — persistent HTTP beacon destination, bare-IP Host header (never resolved via DNS in this capture), custom `CMD=POLL` / `CMD=ENCD` protocol, 308 requests across the capture.

**Malicious domains**
- `quote.checkfedexexp.com` — served the malware-dropping ZIP/JS archive (resolved to 104.21.55.70, 172.67.170.159 — Cloudflare-fronted).
- `business.checkfedexexp.com` — same phishing infrastructure, seen only via DNS resolution in this capture (172.67.170.159, 104.21.55.70); no HTTP transaction to it was captured, so treat as related infra rather than a confirmed delivery point.

**URLs**
- `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` — delivered the ZIP payload.
- `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — delivered the DLL payload via BITS.

**File names**
- `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` — JScript downloader inside the delivered ZIP.
- `knock.pdb` / internal name `knock_v1.1.8` / `release.dll` — internal build artifacts recovered from the DLL payload's PE debug info, not the on-disk delivered filename (the wire filename was the opaque hex string `0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4`).

**File hashes (SHA256, computed locally from objects exported out of the capture)**
- `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5` — the delivered ZIP archive (`managements?...` response body).
- `dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c` — `Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js` (extracted JScript downloader).
- `b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6` — the second-stage PE32+ DLL (`0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4`, delivered from 72.5.43.29).

## Benign context (ruled out, not IOCs)
Bulk of traffic is standard Windows 11 / Edge / Office telemetry and update noise: Microsoft NCSI (`www.msftconnecttest.com`), Windows Update/BITS delivery from legitimate `*.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` / Akamai (23.220.x.x, 199.232.210.172), Bing/MSN/Edge services, SSDP/mDNS/LLMNR local discovery, Adobe ARM update checks (`acroipm2.adobe.com`, `armmf.adobe.com`), OCSP revocation checks, and normal AD/Kerberos/LDAP/SMB traffic to the domain controller at 10.8.15.4.

## Summary
The Windows workstation DESKTOP-H8ALZBV (10.8.15.133, MAC 00:1c:bf:03:54:82), logged in as domain user `plucero`, was infected after browsing to the fake FedEx-tracking site `quote.checkfedexexp.com`, which served a ZIP containing a heavily padded JScript downloader. That downloader used the Windows BITS service to fetch a 64-bit DLL loader/backdoor (internally named "knock" v1.1.8 per its embedded PDB path) from bare IP 72.5.43.29, which then began persistent, DNS-less HTTP beaconing on port 80 using a custom `CMD=POLL`/`CMD=ENCD` protocol that continued for the remainder of the 33-minute capture.
